units.headline: Invaders remain in Ituna-Itatá despite an order to deploy federal forces
units.summary: Brazilian federal prosecutors say more than 500 people are occupying the Ituna-Itatá Indigenous territory in Pará, opening roads and clearing land with fire. The territory protects isolated Indigenous people. A court ordered federal forces to be deployed within 48 hours on August 26; prosecutors said on September 11 that they had still not arrived. Pará has created an overlapping environmental protection area whose rules permit private housing and livestock farming. Prosecutors say land-grabbers invoke those rules to justify occupation. The federal government has argued that deployment requires state authorisation; prosecutors say federal forces can operate on federal land without it.
units.perspective: Land-grabbers can exploit conflicting protections while changing the land itself. In Ituna-Itatá, occupiers invoke state rules permitting housing and ranching on territory protected for isolated Indigenous people. Roads and clearing proceed while federal enforcement is delayed.

units.headline: Nigeria pays former airline workers after a 22-year wait
units.summary: Nigeria’s government says it has paid severance to 2,100 former Nigeria Airways workers and cleared another 600 for payment. The announced settlement covers 18 billion Nigerian naira (about US$14 million) in benefits left unpaid after the state airline’s liquidation in 2004. Finance Minister Taiwo Oyedele said some workers had died waiting; documented next of kin can receive their benefits after legal checks. Payments use the amounts originally recorded, with no inflation adjustment; Oyedele acknowledged that inflation had substantially reduced their value.
units.perspective: After a 22-year wait, the payment has lost much of its purchasing power. With no inflation adjustment, the workers bear the financial cost of the government’s delay.

units.headline: Assam must compensate families after deportations blocked court challenges
units.summary: Indian authorities expelled two women to Bangladesh before they could challenge tribunal rulings declaring them foreigners. On September 3, the Gauhati High Court awarded interim compensation of 200,000 Indian rupees (about US$2,100) each to Jahanara Begum’s son and Mumtaz Begum’s husband. In Jahanara’s case, the court said officials failed to provide the tribunal’s ruling and keep her family informed. Across Assam, it told border police to give people declared foreigners a copy of the ruling before detaining them on the day it is issued. Neither order establishes that the women are Indian citizens.
units.perspective: A right to challenge a citizenship ruling offers little protection if officials deport someone before they can use it. To let these women contest the tribunal rulings, the Gauhati High Court is seeking the foreign ministry’s help to find them in Bangladesh and arrange their return.

units.headline: Taiwan enacts a six-year programme for domestically made drones
units.summary: Taiwan has enacted a six-year programme prioritising low-cost, domestically made drones and unmanned vessels. It calls, in principle, for annual budgets totalling 240 billion New Taiwan dollars (about US$7.6 billion), rather than an upfront appropriation. President Lai Ching-te has cited growing Chinese military pressure while calling for drone mass production and supply chains independent of China. A RUSI study warns that replacing Chinese drone components requires manufacturing capacity, not just local assembly.
units.perspective: A country preparing to deter China may still depend on Chinese components for its drones. If those supplies disappear, a cheap weapon can become difficult to replace. Taiwan’s domestic-production push targets that vulnerability, which local assembly alone cannot remove.

units.headline: NSW Police settle lawsuit alleging unlawful bail checks
units.summary: NSW Police have reached a confidential settlement with two mothers whose Aboriginal sons faced repeated bail checks. One mother alleged that 59 of 109 visits breached the court’s conditions, including 25 when no enforcement condition was in force. Police maintain that the checks were lawful, relying on an implied licence to approach a home. The police watchdog has recommended seeking court permission. ABC News cites a study commissioned by the families’ legal team that found Aboriginal young people received 42% more checks on average in the first 30 days after release. The other mother’s racial-discrimination case continues in the Federal Court.
units.perspective: Police can subject one group to much greater scrutiny without writing a separate rule for it. The continuing NSW case asks whether repeated bail checks on Aboriginal children amount to racial discrimination.

units.headline: Morocco reserves regional parliamentary lists for women
units.summary: Morocco’s revised electoral rules reserve regional parliamentary candidacies for women, while leaving local constituencies open to both sexes. If a regional seat becomes vacant, another woman must fill it. New parties must have at least four women among the 12 people filing their founding declaration, and at least 400 among their 2,000 founding members. The legislative election is scheduled for September 23.
units.perspective: Women seeking a political career can face barriers before an election, in the party networks that recruit and promote candidates. Morocco’s requirements for women among new party founders try to widen participation at that earlier stage.

units.headline: Paracatu officials learn of a proposed 1GW data centre from reporters
units.summary: Atlas Renewable Energy has proposed a 1-gigawatt data centre in Paracatu, Minas Gerais. Mongabay and Intercept Brasil report that its planned power capacity exceeds that of all Brazil’s operating data centres combined. In interviews in May, the city-council president and residents learned of it from reporters. Atlas says the project is preliminary and no technical decisions have been made. It proposes supplying the centre from local solar plants where generation has been curtailed, according to the reporting. It has not disclosed its water source or expected consumption. Official water-conflict designations cover about 80% of the municipality, and the proposed site borders one such area.
units.perspective: Electricity can be abundant where water is already contested. Turning unused solar output into data-centre demand may suit the power supplier without suiting the host community.

units.headline: Polish diocese ordered to compensate a woman abused by a priest
units.summary: A Kielce court has ordered the Catholic diocese to pay 550,000 Polish złoty (about US$150,000) to Iwona Dudzik-Osińska, who agreed to be named publicly. She was abused by a parish priest from the age of 12, beginning in 1981. A criminal investigation in 2007 was discontinued because the alleged offences were too old to prosecute. In 2019, the bishop declined to fund therapy from church funds but later gave her money from his personal account. The July civil judgment, reported on September 2, can still be appealed.
units.perspective: An abuse survivor seeking redress can be left dependent on an official’s personal generosity. The Kielce judgment makes the diocese itself responsible for compensation, giving her a claim against the institution.
